# Provenance: tests/fixtures/render_neutral/

Every byte under this directory is generated by
`rm-mcp/tests/gen_neutral_fixtures.py`, run locally, with no reMarkable
device or cloud account involved. Nothing here is copied from
`tests/fixtures/render/` (the private corpus), from `tools/rm_snapshots/`,
from any drain output, or from the device.

What each fixture actually is:

- `shapes_clean/hexagon_and_grid` -- two native (no-PDF) pages: a regular
  hexagon (a "benzene ring" outline, six points around a centre) and a grid
  of four short horizontal line strokes. Point coordinates are computed in
  `gen_neutral_fixtures.py` (`_hexagon`, `_hline`) from fixed centres/radii
  hardcoded in that script -- not traced from, or derived from, any real
  handwriting.
- `shapes_artifact/engineered_jumps` -- two native pages, each one stroke
  built as a short clean run of points followed by a deliberately large
  jump at high simulated pen pressure -- the rmscene 0.8.0 stroke-merge
  connector signature (see `rm_render_page.py::detect_stroke_merge`),
  engineered directly rather than harvested from an affected real page.
- `pdf_paper/lorem` -- one PDF-backed page. The PDF itself is hand-built by
  `gen_neutral_fixtures.py::build_lorem_pdf` (raw PDF object/xref bytes, no
  external PDF library) and contains only the Wikipedia-standard Lorem
  Ipsum placeholder text (`LOREM` list in that script) -- not a third-party
  academic PDF, not any document from Zotero. The one annotation stroke on
  it is a small synthetic mark placed via the documented PDF_RM_SCALE
  affine relationship (`rmscene = PDF_RM_SCALE * pdf_point + offset`), so
  the fixture exercises that exact transform without needing a real
  calibration session.

`labels.json`'s `expected_*` fields are computed by calling the shipped
`detect_stroke_merge()` against the just-written `.rm` bytes at mint time --
not hand-typed -- so they cannot drift from what the detector actually
produces on this corpus.

To confirm no drift back in: this directory is regenerated by deleting it
and re-running `gen_neutral_fixtures.py`, which is exactly what happened to
produce the committed copy. `git diff` on a re-run is the neutrality check --
a real change would only ever touch this script, never introduce a file the
script didn't write.
